newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Pyongyang agrees to launch Korean peace process.
newsitem.headline: Pyongyang agrees to launch Korean peace process.

text.p: North Korea has agreed to help arrange four-nation peace talks aimed at closing the books on the 1950-53 Korean War, South Korean government sources said on Wednesday.

"Pyongyang has accepted a suggestion that senior officials from the two Koreas, the United States and China meet around early August to set an agenda and other details for the peace talks," one source said.
Wednesday marked the 47th anniversary of the outbreak of the Korean conflict.

U.S. President Bill Clinton and South Korean President Kim Young-sam proposed in April last year that the four nations work out a peace settlement to replace the now-fraying ceasefire pact that ended hostilities.
North Korea said in a Wednesday commentary monitored in Tokyo that it would be ready for peace discussions "as long as the enemies do not provoke a war..."
The report in the official Rodong Sinmun said Pyongyang would pursue peace through negotiations, but it added:

"The Korean People's Army...is keeping a sharp eye on every move of the warmongers who are outwardly calling for 'four-way talks' to secure peace and security while waiting for a chance to trigger a war of aggression against the North."

North Korean watchers said acceptance of peace talks represented a reversal of North Korea's previous stand that any treaty to secure peace on the Korean peninsula must be signed directly by Washington and Pyongyang, excluding South Korea.
Government sources said the North informed the United States and South Korea of the compromise on Tuesday.
The sources said senior officials from the two Koreas and the United States would first meet in New York early next week to announce an accord for the "preparatory talks".

There was no official confirmation, but Seoul foreign ministry spokesman Lee Kyu-hyung said: "There will be an announcement on four-way peace talks at 10:00 p.m. (1300 GMT) today." A similar announcement was due in Washington at the same time, he added.
"North Korea's acceptance of the peace talks underlines how serious its food problem is," said Lee Ki-won, vice president at the independent Institute of North Korea Studies.
"The North needs to ease its food shortage to allow its leader Kim Jong-il to formally take over power," he said.

On July 8, North Korea marks the third anniversary of the death of state founder Kim Il-sung, a milestone that analysts say could clear the way for his son, Kim Jong-il, to take over as head of the state and the ruling Workers Party.
The two posts have been left vacant since Kim's death.
North Korea in April agreed in principle to join the four-nation talks but made its participation conditional on large-scale food aid and an easing of U.S. trade sanctions.
South Korea and the United States have said such assistance could be discussed during peace talks.
"I believe Seoul and Washington have agreed to talk about food aid as soon as the peace talks begin," Lee Ki-won said.
Paik Hak-soon, research fellow at the Sejong Institute, a private think-tank, said the conciliatory gesture by the North was "an inevitable choice" to ease economic stress and the threat of famine.
But Paik predicted a long, painful process before the two Koreas could achieve dtente or implement steps to ease tensions on one of the world's last Cold War frontiers.
"The North will seek bilateral deals with the U.S. to overcome its economic woes and guarantee its survival before considering co-operation with the South," he added.
Seoul officials said humanitarian efforts by the United States and South Korea to help stave off a catastrophe in the North might have encouraged Pyongyang to compromise.

The United States has pledged $25 million and South Korea $16 million in response to the United Nations World Food Programme's most recent appeal for 203,000 tonnes, or $95.5 million, of food for North Korea.
